Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette: Sofía is a 74-year-old Latina pharmacist who has been struggling with symptoms following prolonged physical abuse by her former romantic partner. Her journey to seeking help began over several months, during which she gradually withdrew from the world around her. The abuse was relentless and often occurred when they were alone at home. Each incident left Sofía feeling utterly defenseless and ashamed. The sounds of doors slamming became a trigger for her, reminding her vividly of those moments of violence. Family-related comments also triggered memories, as each comment on family dynamics dredged up the shame she felt about her marriage. Even attempts at emotional closeness with others were met with intense discomfort and fear. Sofía had come to believe that she was no longer capable of doing the things that once defined her. This belief stemmed from how weak she felt in those moments of abuse, a feeling that lingered long after the physical violence ceased. She also began to lose faith in people and life itself. The constant reminders of what happened made it difficult for her to maintain any sense of normalcy or trust. The sounds of doors slamming would often cause her body to tense up, ready to react to perceived danger. This alertness extended beyond just the sound; she found herself feeling on guard even inside her own home, constantly listening for signs that someone was entering her space. When such triggers activated these bodily sensations, memories of those terrifying moments replayed in her mind, often as vivid snapshots. The shame she felt during these recollections further reinforced her negative beliefs about herself. Sofía's avoidance behaviors began to take hold as a way to manage the overwhelming anxiety and fear that accompanied these triggers. She found it increasingly difficult to pay attention to or look at her own body, which had become a source of distress rather than strength. Allowing herself to feel any strong emotion was equally challenging; she felt better if she could numb those feelings altogether. As a result, she began avoiding other people and interactions that might trigger memories. This cycle intensified over time. Her negative appraisals fueled her maladaptive strategies, which in turn reinforced the triggers and exacerbated her intrusive thoughts and bodily sensations. She started to isolate herself at work, finding it difficult to engage with colleagues or patients. The pharmacists' counter became a place of stress rather than routine; even the sound of someone approaching could trigger intense anxiety. Sofía's marriage suffered as well. Her husband noticed that she had become distant and seemed constantly on edge, though he did not fully understand why. He tried to offer support but often felt rebuffed by her withdrawal, leading to a sense of frustration and misunderstanding between them. The combination of these factors led Sofía to finally seek help. What frightened her most was the fear that she would never feel safe again, that the memories and triggers would always control her life. She hoped for a chance to reclaim some semblance of normalcy and faith in herself and others. Despite her fears, she felt compelled to take this step towards healing, hoping it could provide the relief and understanding she so desperately needed.
